name: Amos
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. Amos prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel in the reign of Jeroboam II (about 786–746 BC), probably around 760 BC. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, as reported in the published editions, portions of Amos are preserved in the Qumran manuscripts of the Twelve Prophets (4QXII-c, 4QXII-g, and others), in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll (Mur 88), and in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr); these generally support the Masoretic Text. The combination ʾAdonay YHWH, frequent in Amos, is rendered “the Lord Yahweh.” Verse numbers in Amos are the same in English and Hebrew.

verses.text: The words of Amos, one of the sheep breeders{a} of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.{b}

He said:
“Yahweh roars from Zion
and from Jerusalem lifts his voice;
the shepherds’ pastures mourn,
and the summit of Carmel withers.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Damascus,
yes, for four,{c} I will not turn it back;
because with sledges of iron
they threshed Gilead.

So I will hurl a fire at Hazael’s dynasty,
and it will devour Ben-hadad’s strongholds.{d}

I will smash Damascus’s gate bolt,
and remove the king{e} who sits in the Valley of Aven
and the scepter-bearer in Beth-eden;
and Aram’s population will be deported to Kir,”
says Yahweh.

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Gaza,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they carried off whole communities{f} as captives
to hand them over to Edom.

So I will send a fire upon the wall of Gaza,
and it will consume her fortresses.

I will remove the king of Ashdod,
and the scepter-bearer of Ashkelon;
I will strike Ekron with my hand,
and the Philistines who remain will die,”
says the Lord Yahweh.

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Tyre,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they delivered up whole communities to Edom
and did not remember the covenant of brothers.

So I will send a fire upon the wall of Tyre,
and it will consume her fortresses.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Edom,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because he hunted his brother{g} with the sword
and stifled all compassion;
his anger tore without ceasing,
and he kept his fury forever.

So I will send a fire upon Teman,
and it will consume the fortresses of Bozrah.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of the Ammonites,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead
to widen their own border.

So I will set Rabbah’s{h} wall ablaze,
and the fire will devour her strongholds,
amid war cries on the day of combat,
amid a gale on the day of the tempest.

Into exile their king{i} shall go,
he and his princes with him,”
says Yahweh.

notes.text: Hebrew noqedim, used also of Mesha king of Moab (2 Kings 3:4); perhaps an owner or manager of flocks rather than a simple herdsman (compare 7:14). Tekoa was a village about 10 miles (16 kilometers) south of Jerusalem.
A major earthquake remembered long afterward (Zechariah 14:5); archaeological evidence at several sites, including Hazor, suggests a date of about 760 BC.
A numerical saying meaning “for sin upon sin,” building to a climax (compare Proverbs 30:15–31). “It” is probably the punishment.
Hazael and his son Ben-hadad were kings of Aram (Syria) in the ninth century BC (2 Kings 8:7–15; 13:3, 24).

Or “the inhabitants.” Aven (“wickedness”) and Beth-eden (“house of delight”) may be mocking names. Kir was the original homeland of the Arameans (9:7); they were exiled there by Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BC (2 Kings 16:9).
Hebrew “a complete exile,” sparing no one; likewise in verse 9.
Edom descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob (Genesis 25:19–34; 36:1).
The capital of Ammon, the site of modern Amman in Jordan.
Or “Milcom,” the god of the Ammonites (so some Greek manuscripts; compare Jeremiah 49:3).

verses.text:
So I will send a fire upon Moab,
and it will consume the fortresses of Kerioth;{b}
Moab will die amid tumult,
with shouting and the blast of the horn.

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Judah,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they have rejected the law of Yahweh
and have not kept his statutes,
and their lies{d} have led them astray,
the lies after which their fathers walked.

So I will send a fire upon Judah,
and it will consume the fortresses of Jerusalem.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Israel,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they sell the righteous for silver,
and the needy for a pair of sandals—

they stretch out beside every altar
on garments taken in pledge,{f}
and in the house of their God they drink
the wine of those who have been fined.

“Yet I was the one who wiped out the Amorites ahead of them,
though they stood as tall as cedars
and were as sturdy as oak trees;
I wiped out their fruit on top
and their roots below.

And it was I who brought you up out of the land of Egypt
and led you forty years in the wilderness,
to take possession of the land of the Amorite.

I raised up prophets from among your sons,
and Nazirites from among your young men.{g}
Is that not so, people of Israel?”
declares Yahweh.

“But you gave the Nazirites wine to drink,
and you ordered the prophets,
‘You shall not prophesy.’

The stoutest-hearted among the mighty
shall run away naked in that day,”
declares Yahweh.

notes.text: A desecration of the dead, denying the king rest in his grave.
A city of Moab, mentioned also on the Mesha Stone (about 840 BC).
That is, the king or chief ruler.
That is, their false gods.
Or “who pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor,” that is, who covet even the dust the poor put on their heads in mourning.
The law required that a cloak taken in pledge be returned by nightfall (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:12–13).
People under a vow of separation to God, who abstained from wine (Numbers 6:1–21; Judges 13:4–5).
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; perhaps “I will make you totter” or “I will split the ground beneath you.”

verses.text: Listen to this message Yahweh has announced against you, Israelites, against the entire clan I led out of Egypt:

Do two walk together
unless they have arranged to meet?

Does a lion roar in the forest
when he has no prey?
Does a young lion cry out from his den
unless he has caught something?

Does a bird fall into a snare on the ground
when there is no bait{b} for it?
Does a trap spring up from the ground
when it has taken nothing?

Is a horn blown in a city
and the people not tremble?
Does disaster come to a city
unless Yahweh has done it?

Announce to the strongholds of Ashdod{d}
and to the strongholds of Egypt,
“Gather on Samaria’s hills
and witness the great panic inside her
and the cruelty within her.”

“They do not know how to do right,” declares Yahweh,
“those who store up violence and robbery in their fortresses.”

Therefore this is what the Lord Yahweh declares:
“An enemy will encircle the country;
he will pull down your defenses,
and your strongholds will be looted.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“As a shepherd snatches out of the lion’s mouth
a pair of legs or a piece of an ear,{e}
so will the children of Israel be snatched away, those who sit in Samaria
on the edge of a couch
and on the cushions{f} of a bed.”

“Hear and testify against the house of Jacob,”
declares the Lord Yahweh, the God of Armies,{g}

“For in the day I call Israel to account for his crimes,
I will also deal with the altars of Bethel;
the altar’s horns{h} will be lopped off
and drop to the ground.

I will strike the winter house along with the summer house,
and the houses of ivory{i} will perish,
and the great houses will come to an end,”
declares Yahweh.

notes.text: That is, chosen and cared for (compare Genesis 18:19).
Or “no trap.”
Hebrew sod, the confidential deliberation of a council (compare Jeremiah 23:18, 22).
The Septuagint reads “Assyria.”
A shepherd brought such remains to prove that an animal had been killed by a wild beast and not stolen (Exodus 22:13).
The meaning of the Hebrew word (demesheq) is uncertain; traditionally “Damascus,” perhaps “damask” or “the leg.”
Hebrew ʾelohe hatstseḇaʾoth, traditionally “God of hosts,” the God who commands the armies of heaven and of Israel.
The projections at the four corners of the altar, which a fugitive might grasp for sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50).
Houses with ivory inlay; many carved ivories of this period have been excavated at Samaria.

verses.text:
Hear this word, you cows of Bashan{a}
who are on the mountain of Samaria,
who oppress the poor, who crush the needy,
who say to your lords,{b} “Bring, and let us drink!”

The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his holiness
that the days are surely coming upon you
when they will take you away with hooks,
the last of you with fishhooks.

And you will go out through the breaches,
each straight ahead,
and you will be cast out toward Harmon,”{c}
declares Yahweh.

burn leavened bread as a thank offering,
and announce your freewill offerings, make them known;
for that is what you love, people of Israel!”
declares the Lord Yahweh.

“I gave you cleanness of teeth{e} in all your cities,
and lack of bread in all your places;
but you have not come back to me,”
declares Yahweh.

Two or three towns staggered to another town
to drink water and could not get enough;
but you have not come back to me,”
declares Yahweh.

“I overthrew some of you,
as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,
and you were like a burning stick snatched from the fire;
but you have not come back to me,”
declares Yahweh.

For look—the one who shapes the mountains and creates the wind,
who tells mankind what he is thinking,{f}
who turns dawn to darkness
and strides upon the high places of the earth—
Yahweh, the God of Armies, is his name!

notes.text: Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for its rich pastures and well-fed cattle (Deuteronomy 32:14; Psalm 22:12). The phrase is addressed to the wealthy women of Samaria.
Hebrew ʾadonehem, “their lords,” that is, their husbands (compare Genesis 18:12).
The meaning is uncertain; perhaps a place name, or (with a slight change) “Mount Hermon.”
The law required tithes yearly or every three years (Deuteronomy 14:22–29); Amos mocks their zeal.
That is, nothing to eat.
Or “what his own (God’s) thought is.” Verse 13 is the first of three hymn fragments in Amos (compare 5:8–9; 9:5–6).

verses.text: Hear this word, which I lift up over you as a lament, house of Israel:

“Fallen, no more to rise,
is the young woman Israel;{a}
forsaken on her own soil,
with no one to raise her up.”

For this is what the Lord Yahweh says:
“The city that marched out a thousand strong
will have a hundred left,
and the one that marched out a hundred strong
will have ten left, for the house of Israel.”

For this is what Yahweh says to the house of Israel:
“Seek me and live;

Look for Yahweh, and you will live,
or he will sweep through Joseph’s house like a blaze,
and it will burn with nobody able to put it out at Bethel—

you who turn justice into wormwood{d}
and fling righteousness to the ground!

He who made the Pleiades and Orion,{e}
who turns deep darkness into morning
and darkens day into night,
who calls for the waters of the sea
and pours them out on the face of the earth—
Yahweh is his name—

who flashes destruction upon the strong,
so that destruction comes upon the fortress.

They hate the one who reproves in the gate,{f}
and they loathe the one who speaks with integrity.

Because you stamp on the poor
and extract grain taxes from them,
you have built mansions of carved stone,
yet you will never live in them;
you have set out lovely vineyards,
yet you will never drink the wine.

For I am aware of your many rebellions
and your enormous sins—
you oppress the innocent, accept payoffs,
and push the poor aside in court.

So the wise keep quiet at such a time,
because the times are wicked.

Seek good and not evil,
that you may live;
and so Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be with you,
as you have said.

Hate evil and love good,
and establish justice in the gate;
it may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies,
will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.

So this is what Yahweh, the God of Armies, the Lord, says:
“Wailing will fill every plaza,
and in every street they will cry, ‘Oh no! Oh no!’
Farmers will be summoned to grieve,
and professional mourners{g} to wail;

and in all vineyards there will be wailing,
for I will pass through your midst,”
says Yahweh.

Disaster for you who yearn for Yahweh’s day!
What will Yahweh’s day mean for you?
It will be dark, not bright—

as when a man escapes a lion
only to be met by a bear,
or goes indoors, rests a hand on the wall,
and is bitten by a snake.

Is not the day of Yahweh darkness, not light,
gloom with no brightness in it?

“I hate, I reject your festivals,
and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies.{h}

Though you bring me whole burnt offerings and your gifts of grain,
they will not please me;
the fat beasts of your peace offerings
I will not regard.

Remove from my presence the clamor of your songs;
I will not hear the music of your lyres.

Instead, let justice surge like the waters,
and righteousness like a stream that never fails.{i}

“Was it sacrifices and grain offerings that you brought me
those forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?

therefore I will send you into exile beyond Damascus,”
says Yahweh, whose name is the God of Armies.

notes.text: Hebrew “the virgin Israel,” a poetic personification of the nation. Verse 2 is in the limping rhythm of the Hebrew funeral lament (qinah).
A wordplay in Hebrew: haggilgal galoh yigleh.
Hebrew “will become aven (wickedness, nothingness),” alluding to the name Beth-aven (see the note at Hosea 4:15).
A bitter-tasting plant, used figuratively for what is poisonous (compare 6:12).
Hebrew kimah and kesil, two constellations, probably the Pleiades and Orion (compare Job 9:9; 38:31).
The open area at the city gate where the elders sat to hear legal cases; likewise in verses 12 and 15.
Professional mourners, often women (Jeremiah 9:17–20).
Hebrew “I will not smell,” alluding to the pleasing aroma of sacrifice (Leviticus 26:31).
Hebrew naḥal ʾethan, a wadi that does not dry up in summer.

Sakkuth and Kaiwan are Mesopotamian names for the planet Saturn, worshiped as a god. The Hebrew vowels (Sikkuth, Kiyyun) may be a deliberate distortion modeled on shiqquts, “detestable thing.” The Septuagint reads “the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan,” and is quoted in Acts 7:42–43. The verse may also be read as past: “You carried Sakkuth…”

verses.text:
Disaster for those lounging comfortably in Zion
and those feeling safe on Samaria’s mountain,
the famous leaders of the foremost nation,
the ones Israel’s people turn to!

You who put off the day of disaster
bring near the seat of violence.

They lie on beds of ivory
and sprawl on their couches;
they eat lambs from the flock
and calves from the stall.

They improvise{b} to the sound of the harp;
like David they devise for themselves instruments of song.

They drink wine from bowls
and anoint themselves with the finest oils,
but they do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph.

So now they shall go into exile at the head of the exiles,
and the feasting of the loungers shall be gone.{c}

The Lord Yahweh has sworn by himself, declares Yahweh, the God of Armies:
“I abhor the pride of Jacob
and hate his fortresses;
and I will hand over the city and everything in it.”
If ten men remain in one house, they will die.

And when a relative,{d} the one who burns the dead, picks up the body to carry it out of the house, he will say to whoever is in the innermost parts of the house, “Is anyone else with you?” and he will say, “No.” Then he will say, “Hush! We must not mention the name of Yahweh.”

For look, Yahweh commands,
and the great house will be struck into fragments,
and the small house into splinters.

Do horses run on rocks?
Does one plow the sea with oxen?{e}
But you have turned justice into poison
and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood—

“For look, I am raising up against you a nation, house of Israel,”
declares Yahweh, the God of Armies,
“and they will oppress you from Lebo-hamath{g}
to the Brook of the Arabah.”

notes.text: Calneh and Hamath, cities in northern Syria, and Gath, a Philistine city, were all conquered in the eighth century BC. Some reverse the last line: “Is your territory greater than theirs?”
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; perhaps “strum” or “babble.”
Hebrew marzeaḥ, a feast or banqueting association, often connected with funerary rites (compare Jeremiah 16:5).

Hebrew dod, “uncle” or “kinsman.” The phrase that follows (meśarepho) is usually understood as “the one who burns him,” whether in cremation (unusual in Israel) or burning spices in his honor; the Hebrew of the verse is difficult.
So by a different division of the Hebrew letters (babbaqar yam); the Hebrew text reads “Does one plow there with oxen?”
Lo-debar means “nothing,” and Karnaim means “a pair of horns,” a symbol of strength; both were towns in Gilead, apparently recaptured by Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25).
Hebrew “the entrance of Hamath,” the ideal northern border of Israel. The Brook of the Arabah was probably at the southern end of the Dead Sea. Compare 2 Kings 14:25.

verses.text: This is what the Lord Yahweh showed me: he was forming locusts when the late crop{a} was beginning to sprout, the late crop after the king’s mowing.
When the locusts had eaten every green thing in the country, I cried, “Lord Yahweh, please pardon! How will Jacob survive? He is so tiny.”
Yahweh relented concerning this. “It shall not be,” said Yahweh.
The Lord Yahweh showed me this: he was summoning a judgment of fire, and it consumed the vast deep{b} and began to consume the land.
Then I said, “Lord Yahweh, please stop! How can Jacob stand? He is so small.”
Yahweh relented concerning this. “This also shall not be,” said the Lord Yahweh.
He showed me this: there stood the Lord by a wall made true by a plumb line,{c} and a plumb line was in his hand.
Yahweh asked me, “What are you looking at, Amos?” I answered, “A plumb line.” Then the Lord said, “Look, I am placing a plumb line among my people Israel; I will no longer overlook them.

The high places of Isaac will be laid waste,
and the sanctuaries of Israel will be ruined,
and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”
Then Amaziah, priest of Bethel, sent this message to Jeroboam, Israel’s king: “Amos is plotting against you right in the heart of Israel. The country cannot endure everything he says.
For this is what Amos has said: ‘Jeroboam will die by the sword, and Israel will surely go into exile away from its land.’ ”
And Amaziah said to Amos, “Seer, go, run off to the land of Judah, and earn your bread there, and prophesy there;
but never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king’s sanctuary and a royal house.”
Amos answered Amaziah, “I am no prophet, nor a prophet’s son;{d} I am a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs.{e}
But Yahweh took me from following the flock, and Yahweh said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’
Now hear the word of Yahweh. You are saying, ‘Prophesy no more against Israel; stop dripping words{f} against Isaac’s house.’

Therefore Yahweh says: ‘Your wife will become a prostitute in town; your children will be killed by the sword; your land will be surveyed and divided; you yourself will die in a foreign, unclean country,{g} and Israel will certainly be taken from its homeland into exile.’ ”

notes.text: The crop that grew after the spring rains, in about March–April. The king apparently took the first cutting as a tax.
Hebrew tehom, the subterranean waters thought to feed springs and rivers (Genesis 7:11).

Hebrew ʾanak, a word occurring only here (four times). Traditionally “plumb line,” but it is the Akkadian word for “tin,” and some interpret “a wall of tin” as a symbol of weakness or of military defense; the meaning remains debated.
Or “I was no prophet, nor a prophet’s son.” The Hebrew has no verb. “A prophet’s son” means a member of a prophetic guild (compare 2 Kings 2:3–7).
The fruit of the sycamore fig had to be slit or pinched to ripen; it grew in the lowlands, not at Tekoa itself.
Hebrew “drip,” that is, let words fall.
That is, a foreign land.

verses.text: The Lord Yahweh showed me this: a basket of ripe fruit.
He asked, “What are you looking at, Amos?” I answered, “A basket of ripe fruit.” Then Yahweh told me, “The end{a} has arrived for my people Israel; I will no longer overlook them.
The songs of the temple{b} will become wailings on that day,” declares the Lord Yahweh. “The dead bodies will be many, thrown out everywhere. Hush!”

Hear this, you who trample the needy
and would bring the poor of the land to an end,

who say, “When will the new moon pass,
so we can sell our grain?
When will the Sabbath be done,
so we can set out our wheat,
shrinking the measure and inflating the price,{c}
and tipping deceitful balances,

buying the poor with silver
and the destitute for a pair of sandals,
and selling even the wheat sweepings?”

Yahweh has sworn by the pride of Jacob:{d}
“Surely I will never forget any of their deeds.

Will not the land quake because of this,
and all its inhabitants mourn?
Will it not all rise up like the Nile,
heave, and subside like the river of Egypt?”

“Look, the days are coming,” declares the Lord Yahweh,
“when I will send a famine on the land—
not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water,
but of hearing the words of Yahweh.

They will wander from sea to sea,
and from north to east they will run about
seeking the word of Yahweh,
but they will not find it.

On that day the lovely young women and the young men
will faint for thirst.

Those who swear by the guilt of Samaria,{f}
and say, ‘As your god lives, Dan,’
and, ‘As the way of Beersheba lives,’
will fall and never rise again.”

notes.text: A wordplay in Hebrew between qayits, “summer fruit,” and qets, “end.” The fruit was gathered in August–September.
Or “palace.”

Hebrew “making the ephah small and the shekel great,” that is, giving short measure (the ephah was a dry measure of about two-thirds of a bushel, or 22 liters) and weighing the buyer’s silver with an overweight shekel (normally about two-fifths of an ounce, or 11.5 grams).
Perhaps a title of God himself (compare 1 Samuel 15:29), or spoken in irony of Israel’s arrogance (6:8).
A total eclipse of the sun was visible in the region on June 15, 763 BC, and is recorded in Assyrian sources.
Or “by Ashimah of Samaria,” a goddess (compare 2 Kings 17:30). Dan and Beersheba were sanctuaries at the northern and southern ends of the land.

verses.text:
Though they burrow into Sheol,
my hand will take them from there;
though they mount to the heavens,
I will pull them down from there.

Though they hide on Carmel’s peak,
I will hunt them out and seize them there;
though they hide from my eyes on the floor of the sea,
I will command the serpent there to bite them.

And if they go into captivity before their enemies,
there I will command the sword, and it will kill them;
I will fix my eyes upon them
for harm and not for good.”

He constructs his upper chambers in the sky
and sets his dome{c} over the earth;
he summons the sea’s waters
and pours them over the land’s surface—
Yahweh is his name.

“Are you not like the Cushites{d} to me,
people of Israel?” declares Yahweh.
“Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt,
and the Philistines from Caphtor,{e}
and the Arameans from Kir?

Look, the eyes of the Lord Yahweh are upon the sinful kingdom,
and I will destroy it from the face of the ground,
except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob,”
declares Yahweh.

“For I am giving the command,
and I will sift Israel’s house among all the nations,
as grain is sifted in a sieve,
and not one pebble will drop to the ground.

All the sinners of my people will die by the sword,
who say, ‘Disaster will not overtake or meet us.’

“On that day I will lift up
David’s collapsed shelter,{f}
mend its cracks,
restore its ruins,
and rebuild it as it was long ago,

I will plant them on their land,
and they will never again be uprooted
from the land that I have given them,”
says Yahweh your God.

notes.text: Or “upon.” The altar is probably that of Bethel.
Hebrew YHWH hatstseḇaʾoth, traditionally “the LORD of hosts,” the God who commands the armies of heaven and of Israel.
Or “his band” or “his bundle”; the meaning of the Hebrew ʾaguddah is uncertain here.
The people of the upper Nile region (ancient Nubia).
Probably Crete.
Hebrew sukkah, a hut or shelter, here a figure for the dynasty or kingdom of David in its weakened state.

Hebrew “over whom my name is called,” marking them as his possession. The Septuagint, reading ʾadam (“humankind”) for ʾedom and yidreshu (“seek”) for yirshu (“possess”), has “so that the remnant of humankind, and all the nations upon whom my name is called, may seek me.” James quotes the verses in this Greek form at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16–17) to support the inclusion of the Gentiles.
Hebrew “will melt.”
Or “restore the fortunes.”
